Prealgebra · Lesson 11.7

Circles

Solve this lesson →All lessons

Every shape so far has had straight sides you could count and add up. A circle has none. It still has a distance around the outside, called its perimeter, and a space inside, called its area. Both are measured using one number, ππ, which is the same for every circle. Once you know how to use it, you can measure any circle.

Problem
In the diagram above is a circle whose radius is 88. Find its diameter. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The diameter is twice the radius, d=2rd=2r. Read the radius off the diagram above.
  • The radius is 88, so double it.
Show the full solution
The diameter is twice the radius, d=2rd=2r. The diagram above marks the radius as 88, so d=2×8=16.d=2×8=16. The diameter is 1616​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle with diameter 1010. Its circumference is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • The circumference of a circle is C=πdC=πd, where dd is the diameter. Read the diameter off the diagram above.
  • The diameter is 1010, so the circumference is 1010 times ππ. The whole number you report is the one sitting in front of ππ.
Show the full solution
Circumference is ππ times the diameter. The diagram above gives d=10d=10, so C=πd=10π.C=πd=10π. The whole number multiplying ππ is 1010​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle with radius 77. Its circumference is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • Circumference is C=2πrC=2πr. Read the radius off the diagram above and put it in.
  • With r=7r=7 you get 2×7×π2×7×π. Work out the whole number in front of ππ.
Show the full solution
The circumference of a circle is C=2πrC=2πr. The radius in the diagram above is 77, so C=2×7×π=14π.C=2×7×π=14π. That is a whole number times ππ, and the whole number in front is 1414​.
Key idea
Radius, diameter, and circumference. Every point of a circle is the same distance from the center, and that distance is the radius rr. A segment that crosses the circle through the center is the diameter. It is two radii end to end, so d=2rd=2r (and r=d2r=2d​). The distance all the way around the circle is its circumference. It is always the same multiple of the diameter, whatever the size of the circle. That multiple is the number ππ (about 3.143.14). So C=πd=2πrC=πd=2πr. With a whole-number radius the circumference comes out as a whole number times ππ, like 14π14π. Leave it in that form and give the whole number in front.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle with radius 66. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • Area of a circle is A=πr2A=πr2. Read the radius off the diagram above and square it.
  • With r=6r=6 you get 6262. The whole number multiplying ππ is that value.
Show the full solution
The area of a circle is A=πr2A=πr2. Read the radius 66 off the diagram above and square it. A=π×62=36πA=π×62=36π The area is 36π36π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 3636​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle with diameter 1414. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • The area formula uses the radius, not the diameter, so first find the radius from d=2rd=2r.
  • With the radius in hand, use A=πr2A=πr2 and read off the whole number sitting in front of ππ.
Show the full solution
Halve the diameter to get the radius, r=142=7r=214​=7. Then A=πr2=π⋅72=49π,A=πr2=π⋅72=49π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 4949​. The area formula always runs on the radius, so a diameter has to be halved before it goes in.
Key idea
Area of a circle. Slice a circle into many thin wedges and lay them in a row, alternating point up and point down. They form a shape very close to a parallelogram with base πrπr (half the way around) and height rr. Its area is base times height, πr×rπr×r, so the area of a circle is A=πr2A=πr2. Like the circumference, the answer is a whole number times ππ, and you give that whole number, so an area of 36π36π is answered 3636. If you are given the diameter, halve it to get rr first.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle whose circumference is 26π26π, with the radius marked by a question mark. Find the radius. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The circumference of a circle is C=2πrC=2πr. Set that equal to 26π26π.
  • From 2πr=26π2πr=26π, cancel the ππ on both sides to get 2r=262r=26, then divide by 22.
Show the full solution
Circumference is C=2πrC=2πr, and here it equals 26π26π, so 2πr=26π.2πr=26π. Cancel the ππ on both sides to get 2r=262r=26, then divide by 22. The radius is 1313​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a circle whose area is 64π64π. Find the radius. Give the number of units.
Show a hint
  • The area of a circle is A=πr2A=πr2. Set that equal to the area you are given, 64π64π, and cancel the ππ from both sides.
  • You are left with r2=64r2=64. Ask which number times itself gives 6464.
Show the full solution
The area is A=πr2A=πr2, and here it equals 64π64π, so πr2=64π.πr2=64π. Cancel the ππ on both sides to get r2=64r2=64. The number that squares to 6464 is 88, so r=8r=8​.
Key idea
Finding the radius from a circumference or area. The circle formulas also work backward. Given a circumference or an area written as a whole number times ππ, set the formula equal to it and divide both sides by ππ. For a circumference, 2πr=20π2πr=20π becomes 2r=202r=20, so r=10r=10. For an area, πr2=49ππr2=49π becomes r2=49r2=49, so r=7r=7.
Problem
In the diagram above is a semicircle with radius 88. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • A semicircle is half a circle, so its area is half of a full circle's area, 12πr221​πr2. Read the radius off the diagram above.
  • Square the radius 88 to get 6464, then take half of 64π64π. The answer is the whole number left in front of ππ.
Show the full solution
A semicircle is half a circle, so its area is half of the full circle's πr2πr2. With radius 88, A=12πr2=12×π×64=32π.A=21​πr2=21​×π×64=32π. We leave the answer in terms of ππ, so the area is 32π32π and the whole number is 3232​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a quarter circle with radius 1010. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • A quarter circle is a fourth of a full circle, so its area is 14πr241​πr2. Read the radius off the diagram.
  • Square the radius first, then take a fourth of it. With r=10r=10 you get r2=100r2=100.
Show the full solution
A quarter circle is one fourth of a full circle, so its area is 14πr241​πr2. With r=10r=10, A=14πr2=14×π×100=25π.A=41​πr2=41​×π×100=25π. The area is 25π25π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 2525​.
Problem
In the diagram above is a ring, the shaded space between an outer circle of radius 1010 and an inner circle of radius 66. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • The ring is what's left when you cut the small circle out of the big one, so its area is πR2−πr2πR2−πr2 with R=10R=10 and r=6r=6.
  • Find each area on its own first. The big circle is π×102π×102 and the small one is π×62π×62, then subtract.
Show the full solution
A ring is the big circle with the small circle removed, so its area is the difference of the two areas. The big circle has area π×102=100ππ×102=100π and the small circle has area π×62=36ππ×62=36π. Subtract to get what's left in the ring. 100π−36π=64π100π−36π=64π The area is 64π64π, so the whole number is 6464​.
Problem
In the diagram above are two pizzas, a small one of radius 66 and a large one of radius 1212. How many times as much pizza (area) is the large one? Give the number.
Show a hint
  • Area grows with the radius squared, since A=πr2A=πr2. Start by comparing the radii. How many times bigger is the large radius than the small one?
  • The radius goes from 66 to 1212, so it doubles. When the radius is multiplied by a number, the area is multiplied by that number squared.
Show the full solution
Area is A=πr2A=πr2, so it depends on the radius squared. The radius doubles from 66 to 1212, which multiplies the area by 22=4.22=4. The large pizza is 44​ times as much. Checking directly, the small pizza is 36π36π and the large one is 144π144π, which is 44 times as big.
Key idea
Parts of a circle, and scaling. Part of a circle has area πr2πr2 times the fraction of the circle it covers. A semicircle is 12πr221​πr2 and a quarter circle is 14πr241​πr2. A ring is the flat band between an outer circle of radius RR and an inner circle of radius rr. Its area is the big circle minus the small one, πR2−πr2πR2−πr2. Because area depends on the radius squared, growing the radius by a factor multiplies the area by the square of that factor. Double the radius and the area is 22=422=4 times as big. Triple it and the area is 32=932=9 times as big.
Fun fact
The number ππ never ends and never falls into a repeating pattern. Its digits run on forever with no rhythm, which makes it an irrational number, and computers have now chased it out to trillions of places past the decimal point. It is famous enough to have its own holiday. Every March 14, written 3/14 in the United States, is celebrated as Pi Day, and a few devoted fans memorize thousands of its digits just for the fun of it.
Problem
In the diagram above, the small circular garden has radius 1010 and needs 30003000 seeds to fill it. The larger garden has three times that radius. How many seeds does it need to fill? Give the number of seeds.
Show a hint
  • Area grows with the square of the radius. If the radius is multiplied by 33, the area is multiplied by 3232.
  • Work out 3232, then multiply the number of seeds for the small garden by that factor.
Show the full solution
Seeds needed match the area, and the area of a circle depends on the radius squared. Tripling the radius multiplies the area by 32=9.32=9. So the larger garden needs 99 times as many seeds as the small one, 9×3000=27000.9×3000=27000. The larger garden needs 2700027000​ seeds.
Problem
In the diagram above is a dartboard of three circles with radii 44, 66, and 99. Find the area of the outer ring, the shaded space between the radius-66 circle and the radius-99 circle. That area is a whole number times ππ. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show a hint
  • A ring is a big circle with a smaller one punched out of the middle. Its area is the outer circle's area minus the inner circle's area, πR2−πr2πR2−πr2. Here the innermost radius-44 circle is a distraction, and the outer ring only uses R=9R=9 and r=6r=6.
  • Work out each area on its own first. The big circle has area π×92π×92, and the circle you subtract has area π×62π×62. Then subtract the whole numbers in front of ππ.
Show the full solution
The outer ring is the radius-99 circle with the radius-66 circle taken out, so subtract the two areas. The big circle has area π×92=81ππ×92=81π and the one removed has area π×62=36ππ×62=36π, so 81π−36π=45π.81π−36π=45π. The whole number multiplying ππ is 4545​. The radius-44 circle sits inside the part already removed, so it never enters the calculation.

Practice these ideas

Practice
In the diagram above is a circle with radius 1111. Its diameter is a length you can read off. Find the diameter. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The diameter runs all the way across a circle, and it is exactly twice the radius, so d=2rd=2r. Here the radius is 1111, so d=2×11=22.d=2×11=22. The diameter is 2222​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle with diameter 88. Its circumference is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
The circumference is the diameter times ππ. Read the diameter off the diagram above, d=8d=8, and use C=πd=8π.C=πd=8π. So the whole number multiplying ππ is 88​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle with radius 99. Its circumference is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
The circumference of a circle is C=2πrC=2πr. Here the radius is 99, so C=2π×9=18π.C=2π×9=18π. Leaving the answer in terms of ππ, the whole number multiplying ππ is 1818​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle with radius 55. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
The area of a circle is A=πr2A=πr2. Read the radius 55 off the diagram above and square it. A=π×52=25πA=π×52=25π The area is 25π25π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 2525​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle with diameter 2020. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
The diameter is 2020, and the radius is half of that, so r=10r=10. Area is πr2πr2, so A=π×102=100π.A=π×102=100π. We leave the answer in terms of ππ and give just the whole number in front, so the answer is 100100​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle whose circumference is 30π30π. Find its radius. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
Circumference is 2πr2πr, and here it equals 30π30π, so 2πr=30π.2πr=30π. Divide both sides by 2π2π to get r=15r=15. The radius is 1515​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a circle whose area is 49π49π. Find its radius. Give the number of units.
Show the solution
The area of a circle is πr2πr2. Here that equals 49π49π, so πr2=49π.πr2=49π. Divide both sides by ππ to get r2=49r2=49. The number that squares to 4949 is 77, so the radius is 77​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a semicircle with radius 1010. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
A semicircle is half a full circle, so its area is half of πr2πr2. With r=10r=10 the radius squared is r2=100r2=100, so A=12πr2=12×100π=50π.A=21​πr2=21​×100π=50π. The area is 50π50π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 5050​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a quarter circle with radius 88. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
A quarter circle covers a fourth of the whole circle, so its area is 14πr241​πr2. Reading the radius off the diagram above, r=8r=8, so r2=64r2=64 and A=14πr2=14×64π=16π.A=41​πr2=41​×64π=16π. We leave the answer in terms of ππ, so the whole number in front of ππ is 1616​.
Practice
In the diagram above is a ring between an outer circle of radius 1313 and an inner circle of radius 55. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
A ring is the big disk with the small disk punched out, so its area is the outer area minus the inner area. Using A=πr2A=πr2 for each, π×132−π×52=169π−25π=144π.π×132−π×52=169π−25π=144π. The area is 144π144π, so the whole number multiplying ππ is 144144​.
Practice
In the diagram above are two circles, one with radius 55 and one with radius 1010. The radius of the larger circle is twice the radius of the smaller. How many times as big as the smaller circle's area is the larger circle's area? Give the number.
Show the solution
Area is πr2πr2, so doubling the radius multiplies the area by 22=4.22=4​. Checking it, the small circle has area π⋅52=25ππ⋅52=25π and the large one has π⋅102=100ππ⋅102=100π, which is 44 times as much. Doubling the radius does not double the area.
Practice
In the diagram above, a small circular flower bed of radius 77 needs 150150 bags of soil to fill it. The larger bed beside it has twice the radius. How many bags of soil does the larger bed need? Give the number of bags.
Show the solution
The area of a circle is πr2πr2, so it grows with the square of the radius. Doubling the radius multiplies the area by 22=422=4. The larger bed covers 44 times the area, so it needs 44 times the soil. 4×150=6004×150=600 The larger bed needs 600600​ bags.
Practice
In the diagram above is a dartboard of three circles with radii 55, 88, and 1212. Find the area of the outer ring, the region between the circle of radius 88 and the circle of radius 1212. Its area is a whole number times ππ. Find that whole number. Give the whole number multiplying ππ.
Show the solution
A ring is one circle with a smaller one taken out of it, so its area is the big area minus the small area, πR2−πr2πR2−πr2. The outer edge is at radius 1212 and the inner edge is at radius 88, so π×122−π×82=144π−64π=80π.π×122−π×82=144π−64π=80π. The area is 80π80π, so the whole number is 8080​.
